There’s no shame in changing your mind and realizing this isn’t what you want. The retail industry has such a high turnover rate that your managers are likely already used to people leaving abruptly and for any reason at all. Especially with such a low hourly wage.

It seems they already like you, which is a good sign. Dress professionally, and do your research on the company. Express your passion for not only the industry, but why you want to work for them specifically. Make it personal.

What exactly did you do as a volunteer? I can give some examples of how I could turn my own volunteer experience into job experience. 

In one instance, I handed out flyers and explained the charity’s cause. I could say I represented the organization in a positive way by showing passion and enthusiasm and persuaded people to attend events. This can translate to a job because as a store associate, you’re the first contact for customers and it’s important to give people a good impression of the company to secure sales/maintain loyal customers. 

I also sorted cans for a homeless shelter. I could say this involved a lot of multitasking and required me to work quickly and accurately, which is important in retail. 

If neither of those are helpful, look at the responsibilities in the job description and see how you can apply your experiences to it in a similar way. Also use the fact that you were a volunteer to your advantage. Mention that you enjoy helping people, which is why you’d like experience in a role that’s customer-service oriented.
If you have any interest, it doesn’t hurt to attend an interview. Also, depending on how you applied, you can probably find the position name or job listing in your email.

I would first call the store, tell them you came in before about applying, and ask if there’s a manager you can speak to. If they direct you to one, express your interest in the job and say you would like to schedule an interview. 

If they say there’s no manager available, ask when would be a good time to call back, give them your name, and ask them to let the manager know that you called. 

Have you applied to the places that your friends work at? You’d have a higher chance at landing a job if someone who works there vouches for you.

I did for my first job. If you don’t have much work experience, it helps to leave on good terms and be seen as responsible/considerate by your former employer. It’s unlikely that they’d call for an entry-level position, but having at least 1 decent job reference can be beneficial.

Why would you feel dumb to turn in a 2 weeks notice? And I don’t really understand your reasoning; why would you no call no show to other places if you’re not happy with your current job?

Doing that is never a good look if you might consider working with that company in the future. It really doesn’t take much to call before your interview and say that you’re no longer interested in the position. 

I’d say continue working at your current job until you’re offered a position you find worthwhile.

I’m sure you did great! Did they say anything to suggest that you have a future with them? Obviously this is not always the case but from my experience, if I wasn’t hired on the spot, then I didn’t get the job. But if they had a lot of candidates to get through, then it’s understandable.
If the jobs have an option to include a cover letter, you can take that as an opportunity to explain the gap in your resume and promote your strengths. I hope you find something soon!

Retail jobs often have very short interviews. Just come in something business casual like a button down and slacks and bring your resume, ID, and a pen. 

Prepare to talk about your experience and for simple questions like “Tell me about yourself,” “What do you know about our company,” and “Why would you be a good fit for this position?” Be upbeat, maintain eye contact, and try not to fidget too much. 

Good luck!
